heuristics.rule: Verify the CIP code before enrolling, not the program name
heuristics.condition: When an international student is evaluating any MS program that might qualify for STEM OPT...
heuristics.action: ...confirm the exact CIP code with the DSO and cross-check it against the DHS STEM OPT Designated Degree Program List before accepting admission
heuristics.because: A program branded as 'Data Analytics' or 'Applied AI' may or may not qualify for STEM OPT depending on its CIP code — the name is marketing, the code is legal reality, and the difference is 24 months of work authorization

heuristics.rule: Use 3-attempt cumulative H-1B probability to set expectations, not single-year odds
heuristics.condition: When an international student is planning around STEM OPT as a pathway to permanent US employment...
heuristics.action: ...calculate the probability of getting zero H-1B selections across all 3 attempts: 1 - (1 - annual_rate)^3, and treat that failure probability as a real scenario requiring a written Plan B
heuristics.because: At ~15% annual entry-level selection rate, roughly 6 in 10 STEM OPT holders will exhaust all 3 attempts without an H-1B — planning only for the success scenario is statistically irresponsible

heuristics.rule: Include opportunity cost in MS ROI or the calculation is fictitious
heuristics.condition: When calculating whether an unfunded MS is financially worth it...
heuristics.action: ...add foregone salary (what you would have earned working instead) to tuition and living costs to get the true investment figure, then divide by realistic annual salary premium
heuristics.because: Students who calculate only tuition underestimate total cost by 40-80%, which systematically makes bad programs look viable — a $80K tuition degree can have a $200K real cost once opportunity cost is included

heuristics.rule: Target large known H-1B sponsors exclusively if you are an international new grad
heuristics.condition: When an international MS student is job-searching with a graduation within 12 months...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize applications to companies with documented high H-1B approval volumes (Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, Google, TCS-tier) and de-prioritize SMEs that rarely sponsor
heuristics.because: Sponsorship requirement — not skill gap — is the primary cause of international students receiving 30% fewer offers; concentrating applications on proven sponsors is a structural fix, not an optimization

heuristics.rule: If country of birth is India or China, treat US permanent residency as effectively unavailable when modeling ROI
heuristics.condition: When an Indian or Chinese national is calculating whether an unfunded US MS makes financial sense...
heuristics.action: ...model the career as ending at H-1B status with no realistic green card path, and recalculate break-even assuming eventual departure or third-country transition
heuristics.because: EB-2/EB-3 backlogs for India and China are 50+ years, meaning even a successful H-1B holder cannot achieve long-term US residency through employment-based pathways in a career-relevant timeframe

heuristics.rule: Ask for program-specific employment data, not school-wide data
heuristics.condition: When evaluating an MS program's career outcomes...
heuristics.action: ...request placement rates and employer names specific to that program cohort for the last 2 years, and verify whether those employers are H-1B sponsors
heuristics.because: School-wide employment statistics aggregate high-performing programs with low-performing ones, making a 30% placement program look acceptable when aggregated with a 90% placement engineering program

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether a student gets 12 or 36 months of work authorization, which changes H-1B attempt count from 1 to 3 and fundamentally alters immigration probability
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Request the exact 6-digit CIP code from the program's DSO and verify it appears on the official DHS STEM OPT Designated Degree Program List before enrolling

decision_factors.why_it_matters: For Indian and Chinese nationals, even a successful H-1B chain leads to a 50+ year green card wait, meaning the entire US career trajectory is built on a visa status that can be terminated — this negates the ROI assumption of long-term US employment
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check current EB-2/EB-3 priority dates for your country of birth on the USCIS Visa Bulletin; if the cutoff date is more than 10 years behind, model as effectively unavailable

decision_factors.why_it_matters: 43% of MS programs have negative lifetime ROI even for domestic students; for international students facing employment gaps and immigration risk, negative-ROI fields become catastrophically negative
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Cross-reference field against FRREOP data: CS/Engineering are reliably positive; Education, Arts, Social Sciences, Humanities are frequently negative; Business/MBA is highly variable

decision_factors.factor: Program-specific employer pipeline to H-1B sponsors
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A program's value for international students is not its ranking but whether it places graduates at companies large enough and willing enough to sponsor H-1B
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask admissions or current students which specific companies recruited on campus in the last 2 years; cross-check those companies against USCIS H-1B disclosure data to confirm sponsorship history

decision_factors.factor: True total cost including opportunity cost
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The break-even timeline — and therefore whether ROI is achievable within a realistic US employment window — depends on total real cost, not sticker tuition
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate: tuition + 2 years living expenses + foregone salary (what you would earn in your home country or current job during those 2 years)

decision_factors.factor: Existing employer relationship with sponsorship intent
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A student with a pre-existing employer who has committed to sponsoring H-1B bypasses the lottery dependency risk that invalidates most international MS ROI calculations
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Confirm in writing — not verbally — whether the employer will sponsor; verbal commitments from managers who cannot authorize HR policy are not reliable

decision_factors.factor: Viability of Plan B without H-1B
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Because ~60% of STEM OPT holders statistically exhaust H-1B attempts, a student without a credible alternative path is taking a 60% chance of an unplanned outcome
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Evaluate concretely: Canadian graduate stream PR eligibility, home country job market with US MS credential, third-country options — vague 'I'll figure it out' is not a plan

decision_factors.factor: Annual salary premium of MS over next-best alternative
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The break-even timeline is salary premium divided into total cost — a small premium means the student must remain employed in the US for many years to recover investment
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research median salary for your specific role with and without MS in your target geography; do not use national averages if you are targeting a specific metro

decision_factors.factor: Employment rate specific to that program cohort
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A 44.6% average international student employment rate means some programs perform far worse; program-level data reveals actual pipeline strength
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Request cohort-specific 6-month employment data from the program; if they cannot or will not provide it, that itself is signal

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Enrolling in an unfunded MS in a non-STEM or borderline-STEM field
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You get 12 months of OPT instead of 36, reducing H-1B attempts from 3 to 1, dropping cumulative selection probability from ~39% to ~15% — the degree's immigration value collapses even if academically equivalent
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who chose programs based on branding or rankings without verifying CIP code, especially in data, analytics, or interdisciplinary programs

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking out loans to fund an unfunded MS in a field with borderline ROI
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The debt must be serviced regardless of employment outcome; if the student fails to get H-1B and returns home, they are repaying a US dollar loan on a home-country salary — which can consume 30-50% of income for a decade
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students from lower-income countries where home-country salaries are a fraction of US debt service requirements

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Targeting small or mid-size employers because they seem more accessible
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: These employers typically cannot or will not sponsor H-1B, meaning any OPT job at such a company is a temporary bridge with no path to the H-1B needed for continued US employment
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students from non-CS fields where big tech is not the default employer pipeline, and first-generation international students without career guidance

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pursuing an unfunded US MS as an Indian or Chinese national
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Even perfect execution — graduating, finding H-1B sponsor, winning lottery — results in indefinite H-1B status with a 50+ year green card wait, meaning the student builds a life in the US with no legal permanence
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Indian and Chinese nationals who model their career assuming eventual permanent residency and make life decisions (marriage, home purchase, children's schooling) on that assumption

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using school-wide employment statistics to evaluate a program
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: High-placement programs in engineering or CS inflate the overall metric, masking 20-40% placement rates in lower-demand programs within the same institution
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students applying to non-CS MS programs at strong CS schools, who assume the school's brand translates uniformly across departments

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing an unfunded MS because 'I couldn't get into a PhD program'
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The MS does not automatically fix whatever prevented PhD admission; if the barrier was research experience or GPA, neither is addressed by coursework alone, making the second PhD application only marginally stronger while the student has spent $100K+
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who view the MS instrumentally as a PhD stepping stone without a concrete plan for what research output the MS will produce

failure_patterns.pattern: Calculating MS ROI using tuition cost only, ignoring opportunity cost and employment probability
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Tuition is a concrete, visible number; opportunity cost and employment risk require probabilistic reasoning that feels speculative — students anchor on the number they can see
failure_patterns.consequence: Students believe they are making a $60-80K investment when the true cost is $150-200K, and they underestimate break-even timelines by 5-10 years
warning_signs: Student describes the investment as 'just the tuition'
Break-even calculation does not mention foregone salary
Student has no salary comparison between MS and non-MS roles in their target market

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming STEM OPT eligibility based on program branding rather than CIP code verification
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Program names like 'Data Science,' 'Business Analytics,' or 'Applied Computing' sound technical and STEM-adjacent; students assume eligibility without checking the legal classification
failure_patterns.consequence: Student enrolls expecting 36 months of work authorization, graduates to 12 months, makes one H-1B attempt instead of three, and faces departure after a single failed lottery at ~15% odds
warning_signs: Student cannot name the program's CIP code when asked
Student has not spoken with the program's DSO about STEM OPT
Program is in a business school but marketed as data/analytics

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating OPT employment as equivalent to domestic employment for career planning
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students focus on getting the degree and getting a job, treating the visa layer as an administrative detail rather than a structural constraint that changes which employers are viable
failure_patterns.consequence: Student accepts OPT role at a company that does not sponsor H-1B, spends 1-2 years there, then faces forced departure or a lateral move under deadline pressure
warning_signs: Student has not researched whether their target employers appear on USCIS H-1B disclosure data
Job search strategy does not filter by employer sponsorship history
Student is targeting companies with under 200 employees in cost-conscious industries

failure_patterns.pattern: Indian and Chinese nationals pursuing unfunded US MS without modeling the EB backlog into their long-term plan
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The green card backlog is abstract and far away; students optimize for the near-term milestone (get the degree, get the job) and defer the long-term problem because it feels distant and unchangeable
failure_patterns.consequence: Student builds 5-10 years of US career, life infrastructure, and identity, then faces the backlog reality with no viable path to permanence and a home-country job market where they are now overpriced and out of network
warning_signs: Student's 10-year plan assumes permanent residency without acknowledging the backlog
Student is from India or China and has not researched current EB priority dates
Student dismisses the backlog as 'something that will get fixed'

failure_patterns.pattern: Pursuing unfunded MS in a negative-ROI field without a non-US-employment scenario
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students in fields like education, social sciences, or arts apply to MS programs because they are passionate about the subject and model success as 'getting the degree and finding a job' — the financial math is never actually run
failure_patterns.consequence: Student graduates with $60-90K in debt, faces a salary of $45-55K with no STEM OPT, fails to find H-1B sponsorship (rare in these fields), and returns home with a degree that does not command a premium in their home market
warning_signs: Student cannot articulate the salary premium the MS will generate
Student's target field rarely appears on H-1B sponsor lists
Student has not compared lifetime earnings with and without the degree

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the exact CIP code for this program, and have you verified it is on the DHS STEM OPT Designated Degree Program List?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student will have 12 or 36 months of work authorization, which determines how many H-1B attempts they get and fundamentally changes the immigration risk profile
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you confirmed this with the DSO in writing, not just from the program website?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This is the single most important verification to do before accepting admission — do you have the DSO's contact information to check this week?

diagnostic_questions.question: What country were you born in?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether long-term US permanent residency through employment is a realistic outcome within a career timeframe — for Indian and Chinese nationals, it is not
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If India or China: have you modeled your career assuming you will be on H-1B status indefinitely with no green card, and does that scenario still make the MS worthwhile?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If other country: what are current EB priority dates for your country, and how does that affect your long-term US residency timeline?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your total cost including living expenses and foregone salary — not just tuition?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student has done a realistic ROI calculation or is anchoring on the sticker price and underestimating the true investment by 50-150%
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the annual salary premium you expect from the MS over your next-best alternative, and how many years of US employment does that require to break even?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Calculate: tuition + living for program duration + what you would have earned working instead — that is your real investment figure

diagnostic_questions.question: Which specific employers recruited from this program in the last two years, and do those employers have a documented history of H-1B sponsorship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the program has a real pipeline to viable employers for international students, versus general employment statistics that may include employers who will not sponsor
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Can you get the names of specific companies, not aggregated placement rates? Have you looked those companies up on USCIS H-1B disclosure data?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the program cannot provide this, that is informative — programs with strong international pipelines can answer this question

diagnostic_questions.question: If you exhaust all H-1B attempts and do not get selected, what is your specific plan?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student has a credible alternative path or is implicitly assuming success in a process where ~60% of STEM OPT holders fail across 3 attempts
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is the plan concrete — Canadian graduate PR application, specific home-country employer, third-country option — or is it 'I'll figure it out at the time'?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: A real Plan B should be evaluated now, before spending $100-200K, not after the H-1B attempts are exhausted

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you pursuing this MS because you could not get into a PhD program, and if so, what specifically will the MS change about your PhD application?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student has a strategic reason to expect the MS to fix the PhD admission barrier, or whether they are spending $100K+ on a degree that will not address the root cause
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What research output — publications, thesis, conference presentations — will you produce during the MS that was missing from your PhD application?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the answer is 'just better GPA' or 'more coursework,' that may not be sufficient — PhD admissions committees weight research experience heavily

industry_realities.common_belief: A master's degree always increases lifetime earnings over not having one
industry_realities.actual_reality: 43% of master's degree programs have negative lifetime ROI, and the median bachelor's degree has higher lifetime ROI (~$160K) than most master's degrees, because it costs less and takes less time
industry_realities.implication: Field selection for an MS is not a preference question — it is a financial risk decision; students in negative-ROI fields are paying for a credential that statistically makes them worse off financially

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting a job in the US after graduation is primarily a skills and networking problem
industry_realities.actual_reality: International students apply to 2x as many jobs but receive 30% fewer offers than domestic students, and the primary cause is sponsorship requirement, not skill gap — this is a structural constraint, not a performance gap
industry_realities.implication: Improving your resume or networking harder does not solve the sponsorship problem; job search strategy must be built around targeting only known H-1B sponsors from the start

industry_realities.common_belief: STEM OPT gives you 3 H-1B attempts, so most people eventually get selected
industry_realities.actual_reality: At entry-level selection rates of ~15%, cumulative probability of at least one selection in 3 attempts is ~39%, meaning approximately 6 in 10 entry-level international graduates with STEM OPT will exhaust all attempts without an H-1B
industry_realities.implication: Plan B is not a pessimistic contingency — it is the statistically more likely outcome for entry-level international graduates and should be planned with equal seriousness to Plan A

industry_realities.common_belief: Any program called 'Data Science,' 'Analytics,' or 'Applied Computing' qualifies for STEM OPT
industry_realities.actual_reality: STEM OPT eligibility is determined by the program's CIP code, not its name or marketing; a Data Analytics MS in a business school may have a non-STEM CIP code and not qualify
industry_realities.implication: Never assume STEM OPT eligibility from the program name — verify the CIP code with the DSO before enrolling, as this decision cannot be easily corrected after the fact

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting H-1B sponsorship from any employer counts the same
industry_realities.actual_reality: Small and mid-size companies often cannot or will not sponsor H-1B due to cost ($2,200–$6,400+ per petition plus attorney fees) and administrative burden; targeting them on OPT leads to a dead end when H-1B is required
industry_realities.implication: For international students, employer size and H-1B sponsorship history must be treated as primary hiring filters, not secondary considerations after role fit and compensation

industry_realities.common_belief: Indian and Chinese nationals who get H-1B sponsorship have solved the immigration problem
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B is a temporary status; EB-2/EB-3 green card backlogs for India and China exceed 50 years at current rates, meaning H-1B holders from these countries cannot realistically achieve permanent residency through employment-based pathways
industry_realities.implication: Indian and Chinese nationals should model their US career as H-1B-capped with no green card endpoint, and evaluate whether that scenario still justifies the investment and life disruption of an unfunded MS

industry_realities.common_belief: The 90-day unemployment limit during OPT is a soft guideline
industry_realities.actual_reality: Exceeding 90 aggregate days of unemployment during standard OPT jeopardizes F-1 status — this is a hard legal limit, not a soft guideline — meaning a student who struggles to find work faces both financial and legal consequences simultaneously
industry_realities.implication: Students should begin job searching before graduation and have employer targets identified, not treat OPT as a gap year with a safety net

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Compares tuition cost to expected salary increase; if the salary goes up, the degree seems worth it
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Calculates total real cost (tuition + living + opportunity cost) divided by realistic annual salary premium, then stress-tests the break-even timeline against employment probability and immigration risk
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A degree that looks positive on tuition-only math can be deeply negative when full cost and employment probability are included; the mistake is made at enrollment and cannot be undone

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Plans to OPT → H-1B → green card, treating each step as a natural progression that happens if you work hard enough
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Models each step as a probabilistic gate with specific failure rates, runs cumulative probability across the chain, and builds a concrete alternative plan for the most likely failure point
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The chain OPT → H-1B → green card has an overall success rate below 20% for most international students; treating it as a deterministic path leads to catastrophic unplanned outcomes

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Evaluates programs based on rankings, brand name, and course curriculum; assumes a well-ranked school with good courses produces good employment outcomes
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Evaluates programs based on CIP code for STEM OPT eligibility, program-specific placement rates with named employers, and whether those employers are documented H-1B sponsors
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Brand name does not transfer to visa sponsorship; a top-ranked program in a field with few H-1B sponsors has worse practical outcomes for international students than a lower-ranked program with a strong big-tech pipeline

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Plans for the success scenario in detail; describes downside scenarios vaguely as 'I'll figure it out' or 'cross that bridge when I come to it'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats the failure scenario (no H-1B after 3 attempts) as a concrete plan that requires the same specificity as the success scenario, because it is the statistically more likely outcome
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: At ~60% failure rate for STEM OPT → H-1B conversion, the downside is the base case; a student without a real Plan B is betting $100-200K on a 40% probability without acknowledging the bet

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Applies broadly to any company with an interesting role and competitive compensation; treats visa sponsorship as something to negotiate after an offer
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Pre-filters the entire job search by documented H-1B sponsorship history; treats any company without sponsorship history as out of scope for primary applications
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: An OPT role at a non-sponsoring employer is a 1-2 year detour that ends in forced departure; the earlier this filter is applied, the less wasted effort and the lower the career disruption risk

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats all international students as facing the same immigration path; does not distinguish between nationalities when modeling long-term US career prospects
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Immediately adjusts the entire career model for Indian and Chinese nationals to account for 50+ year EB backlogs, treating permanent residency as unavailable and re-evaluating whether the US is the right destination at all
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Identical credentials and identical career execution produce radically different long-term outcomes depending on country of birth; ignoring this leads Indian and Chinese nationals to make 10-year life investments in a path that has no legal endpoint
